## A bet on the decisions {#place-your-bet}

::: {.none}
Nine decisions vary on the curve: outcome, predictor, series, predictor form, adjustment, estimator, no-opinion rule, item set and cell weighting

**Which decision moves the estimates most across the `r format(nrow(spec_curve), big.mark = ",")` specifications?**

Write down your guess.
:::

::: notes
Before I show the answer, commit to a guess, since you have made these choices yourselves in the hands-on. Nine decisions vary on the curve, from the outcome scale and the predictor to the scoring of respondents who mention nothing. Which of them moves the estimates most across all eight hundred and sixty-four? The outcome is a common pick, because what 'EU framing' means sounds like the deepest choice, and the measurement decisions are another, since most of us have views about missing answers or about which unemployment series to trust. Write down your answer. [pause, then advance]
:::

## Fork importance {#the-outcome-fork-carries-half-of-everything}

```{r}
#| label: fork-importance
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
# Two readings of each decision on the curve (data/spec_curve_forks.csv): the
# share of the variance of the claim-aligned partial r that its main effect
# carries, and the share of pairs, differing only in that decision, whose two
# members fall in different classes under CR2. Ordered by the share
# of the variance; the estimator in orange, the interactions in grey.
fk <- curve_forks |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    name     = axis_names[axis],
    share    = share / 100,
    crossing = crossing_rate / 100,
    fill     = dplyr::case_when(axis == "estimator" ~ "lead",
                                axis == "interactions" ~ "rest",
                                .default = "axis")
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::if_else(axis == "interactions", -Inf, share)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(name = factor(name, levels = name))
fk_fill <- ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(lead = orange, axis = ncl_blue, rest = grey_mid),
                             guide = "none")
p_share <- ggplot2::ggplot(fk, ggplot2::aes(share, name, fill = fill)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = fmt_pct(share)), hjust = -0.15, colour = ncl_blue,
            fontface = "bold", size = 4.4) +
  fk_fill +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.55), labels = NULL) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "share of the variance", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(15)
p_cross <- ggplot2::ggplot(dplyr::filter(fk, axis != "interactions"), ggplot2::aes(crossing, name, fill = fill)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = fmt_pct(crossing)), hjust = -0.15, colour = ncl_blue,
            fontface = "bold", size = 4.4) +
  fk_fill +
  ggplot2::scale_y_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.85), labels = NULL) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "pairs that change class when it moves alone", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(15) +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_blank())
p_share + p_cross
```

::: {.small}
- The **estimator** carries **`r fmt_pct(fork_of("estimator"))`** of the variance, the predictor `r fmt_pct(fork_of("predictor"))` and the outcome `r fmt_pct(fork_of("outcome"))`; the no-opinion rule, the series, the form and the cell weighting together carry `r fmt_pct(sum(purrr::map_dbl(c("noop", "measure", "pred_form", "cell_weight"), fork_of)))`
- The no-opinion rule carries almost none of the variance and still changes the class of `r fmt_pct(fork_of("noop", "crossing_rate"))` of its pairs
:::

::: {.src}
data/spec_curve_forks.csv: main-effect shares of the variance over the curve, and class changes under CR2 errors clustered by country. The [decision map]({{< var site-url >}}menu.html#map) shows where each decision is made.
:::

::: notes
The estimator accounts for the largest share of the variation on the curve, about forty-one per cent, the predictor comes next at seventeen, and the outcome scale, which many people bet on, carries nine. The estimator is here the choice between two estimands, with or without the year effects, which is why it does so much. The decisions about measurement that occupy so much of the methods literature carry about one per cent between them, and the interactions among decisions about a quarter. The right-hand panel shows how often moving one decision, with the rest held, changes whether a specification clears the CR2 test. The predictor leads there, while the no-opinion rule, with almost no share of the variance, still changes the class of about one pair in twenty-five, so a decision can matter little across the curve and still decide whether your own result is significant. Whoever guessed the estimator takes the point.
:::

## The reference results in the curve {#the-unit-of-analysis-does-the-work}

```{r}
#| label: analyst-placement
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
# The six reference results (data/reference_marks.csv) under three
# conversions of the same statistic: on the degrees of freedom of its own
# inference, where the mark is placed; on the 233 df of the two-way design,
# the common denominator of the conversion lesson; and as the robustness study recorded
# it, drawn only where it differs from the placement, which is PRL47 alone (OA
# has no recorded value). The bands behind are the curve: its full range, its
# middle half and its median (dashed).
conv <- ref_marks |>
  dplyr::select(tag, placed = r_placement, on_233 = r_233, recorded = r_recorded) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(on_233, recorded), names_to = "kind", values_to = "r") |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(r), kind != "recorded" | abs(r - placed) > 0.001) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(dplyr::distinct(ref_marks, tag, r = r_placement) |>
                     dplyr::mutate(kind = "placed")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(kind = factor(kind, levels = c("placed", "on_233", "recorded"),
                              labels = c("own df (placed)", "233 df", "as recorded in the robustness study, where it differs")))
row_levels <- rev(ref_marks$tag)
curve_q <- stats::quantile(spec_curve$r_ca, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
ggplot2::ggplot(conv, ggplot2::aes(r, factor(tag, levels = row_levels))) +
  ggplot2::annotate("rect", xmin = min(spec_curve$r_ca), xmax = max(spec_curve$r_ca),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = plain, alpha = 0.06) +
  ggplot2::annotate("rect", xmin = curve_q[[1]], xmax = curve_q[[3]],
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = plain, alpha = 0.10) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = curve_q[[2]], colour = plain, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = grey_mid, linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(shape = kind, colour = kind), size = 4.2, stroke = 1.1) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = ref_marks, ggplot2::aes(x = 0.14, y = tag,
                                  label = sprintf("%d of %d further below zero", rank, nrow(spec_curve))),
            hjust = 0, size = 4, colour = grey_mid, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 1, 4), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(ink, ink, d_red), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.62, 0.52), breaks = seq(-0.6, 0, by = 0.2),
                     labels = \(x) fmt_num(x, 1)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "partial correlation r", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(15) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left")
```

::: {.small}
- The original study is placed by a refit of its design without its education interactions, as on the curve slide; on its own df PRL47 sits near the weak end, where the robustness study recorded it at `r fmt_num(mark_of("PRL47", "r_recorded"))`, converted on `r format(analysts5$n[analysts5$analyst_id == "PRL47"], big.mark = ",")` respondents
- On 233 df every other result moves, and KEVF1 changes places with KQXUE: the common denominator is a teaching device, worked through in the [conversion lesson]({{< var site-url >}}background.html#sec-recorded) of the background page
:::

::: {.src}
data/reference_marks.csv; each statistic converted as $r = t/\sqrt{t^2 + df}$. The bands are the curve: its range, its middle half and its median.
:::

::: notes
The six reference results appear here with three values each. The filled dot places each on the degrees of freedom of its own inference, as on the curve slide, and the open circle converts the same statistic on two hundred and thirty-three degrees of freedom, those of my own two-way design and the common denominator of the conversion lesson. The red cross marks the value recorded by the robustness study where it differs, which happens only for PRL47, whose z was converted on the number of respondents. The bands behind the dots show the range of the curve, its middle half and its median. I take two things from the chart: the choice of degrees of freedom moves a result about as much as the largest decisions on the menu do, and once the choice counts the units that carry the evidence, the five analysts spread across most of the curve rather than across two orders of magnitude.
:::

## Sign changes by option {#the-sign-flips-are-patterned-not-random}

```{r}
#| label: sign-flips
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.9
# The share of pairs whose two members lie on different sides of zero: for the
# decisions on the curve, pairs that differ only in that decision
# (data/spec_curve_forks.csv); for the options off the curve, each curve
# specification against its twin with the option swapped in
# (data/menu_deviations.csv; the rate repeats the count and is left out).
# Only decisions and options that change at least one sign are drawn.
opt_labels <- menu_opts |> dplyr::select(axis, option, label)
flips <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  curve_forks |>
    dplyr::filter(axis != "interactions") |>
    dplyr::transmute(label = axis_names[axis], sign_changes = sign_changes / 100,
                     where = "decisions on the curve"),
  deviations |>
    dplyr::filter(!on_curve, axis != "se", n_pairs > 0, rule != "identical_to_count") |>
    dplyr::distinct(axis, option, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
    dplyr::left_join(opt_labels, by = c("axis", "option")) |>
    dplyr::transmute(label, sign_changes = sign_changes / 100,
                     where = "options off the curve")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(sign_changes > 0) |>
  dplyr::arrange(sign_changes) |>
  dplyr::mutate(label = factor(label, levels = unique(label)))
ggplot2::ggplot(flips, ggplot2::aes(sign_changes, label, fill = where)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = fmt_pct(sign_changes)), hjust = -0.15, colour = ncl_blue,
            fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  ggplot2::facet_grid(where ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(`decisions on the curve` = ncl_blue,
                               `options off the curve` = d_red), guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.6), labels = NULL) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "pairs whose two members lie on different sides of zero", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(14) +
  ggplot2::theme(strip.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0, colour = ncl_blue, face = "bold"))
```

::: {.small}
- On the curve, `r sum(spec_curve$r_ca > 0)` of the `r format(nrow(spec_curve), big.mark = ",")` specifications lie above zero, all of them GDP growth on the cosmopolitan scale, and `r if (any(spec_curve$r_ca > 0 & spec_curve$sig)) "some" else "none"` with CR2 p < 0.05
- Off the curve the sign changes come from options that change the question: **pooled OLS** brings in the comparison between countries, and the samples **without the bailout countries** or **before the crisis** remove the cases that the claim is about
:::

::: {.src}
data/spec_curve_forks.csv and data/menu_deviations.csv. The [decision map]({{< var site-url >}}menu.html#map) gives the reason for each option, on the curve or off it.
:::

::: notes
On the curve itself there is little to read about signs: sixteen of the eight hundred and sixty-four specifications lie above zero, all of them growth on the cosmopolitan scale, none clearing the CR2 test, and the estimator, which moves the estimates most, changes no signs at all. The sign changes come from options that the review moved off the curve, and they follow a pattern. Pooled OLS, swapped into every specification, changes the sign of half of them, because it brings in the comparison between countries, where the association runs the other way, and leaving out the bailout countries, or keeping only the years before the crisis, changes the sign of about a quarter, because those samples remove the cases that the claim is most about. Each of those options answers another question, which is why it is taught beside the curve rather than on it.
:::
